query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined experimental and simulation approach, employing high-throughput DSC measurements to determine fusion-related properties alongside CALPHAD and atomistic modeling to interpolate across composition space, can accurately and efficiently characterize the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change on melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal-element alloys in homogenized or as-cast form, spanning representative quaternary to senary compositions.
generation.intervention: Perform systematic high-throughput DSC scans to extract melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume changes at melting while simultaneously carrying out CALPHAD and molecular-dynamics simulations to predict and verify these properties across a wide compositional domain.
generation.conditions: Temperatures from subsolidus to above the liquidus (approximately 1000°C–1700°C), under controlled heating/cooling rates that ensure reproducible thermal signals and near-equilibrium transformation paths.
generation.structural_mediator: The synergy of multiple principal element interactions in the solid and liquid, modulated by increasing configurational entropy, local lattice distortions, and potential short-range ordering, dictates the thermodynamics of fusion as revealed by DSC and modeling.
generation.mechanism: Integration of reliable, direct DSC data in a high-throughput format, combined with thermodynamic modeling (CALPHAD) and atomistic simulations (MD), leverages broad composition-phase relations and first-principles-based property calculations, thereby enabling efficient estimation and validation of melting-related thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Measured and simulated melting temperatures are expected to match within approximately ±10°C, with fusion enthalpies/entropies typically predictable to within ±5%, and volume changes at melting accurate to about ±3%, enabling thorough screening of new high-entropy-alloy compositions for high-temperature applications.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC or dilatometry measurements on single-principal-element or simpler alloys, which have limited transferability and narrower composition coverage.
generation.boundary: Accuracy may decline if significant metastable phases, hitherto unknown intermetallics, or severe short-range ordering appear outside existing thermodynamic datasets; iterative refinement of CALPHAD models and continued empirical validation are required in these less-characterized compositional regions.
generation.uncertainty: Localized chemical ordering, phase segregation, or kinetic hindrances in high-entropy alloys at high temperatures could introduce measurement deviations and limit the precision of the predicted thermodynamic values. Additional experiments are needed to quantify such effects in compositionally complex regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Choose multiple quinary HEA compositions with varying principal elements and systematically measure melting properties via DSC across a range of scan rates, while performing parallel CALPHAD and MD-based predictions. Collect in situ diffraction data during melting to detect unexpected phase transitions and measure volume changes using high-temperature dilatometry.
measurements: Melting temperature via DSC onset and peak signal
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion through integrated DSC peaks
Volume changes obtained from high-temperature dilatometry/pycnometry
CALPHAD/MD-derived thermodynamic predictions for each material
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If several cases exhibit significant and consistent discrepancies of more than 20°C in predicted vs. measured melting temperature or more than 10% error in fusion enthalpy/entropy or volume changes, the proposed integrated DSC and computational approach would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available.
